role.altitude: The emergency physician keeps examining, choosing tests, interpreting them, setting priorities, diagnosing and agreeing dispositions; clicking through screens for vitals and history, ordering test by test and typing notes and handovers shrink a little.
skills_to_grow: Checking drafted notes and code suggestions quickly and critically
role.ambitious_version: An emergency physician who has the patient's whole picture on one screen at the bedside and spends the time saved with patients.

tasks.short: Select tests, request them in the record, perform bedside procedures, interpret diagnostic procedures such as laboratory tests, electrocardiograms, emergency ultrasounds and radiographs, and document the findings.

steps.what: Emergency physician selects the diagnostic procedures needed
Emergency physician requests laboratory tests and imaging in the record: test by test today, from an order set after the change
Emergency physician checks the final orders: patient, tests, clinical question and urgency
Emergency physician signs the checked orders, releasing them to the lab and radiology
Emergency physician performs emergency ultrasounds and electrocardiograms at the bedside
Emergency physician interprets the results of the diagnostic procedures
Emergency physician documents the findings in the record

tasks.design: Order sets per presenting complaint, agreed by the department, let the physician request a standard panel in one step and add or drop tests. The physician checks the final orders and signs them once. ECG measurements and ultrasound images flow from the devices into the record, and the physician writes the findings as today. Choosing tests, performing bedside procedures and interpreting stay fully with the physician.

approvals.approved_version: The lab and imaging orders with patient, tests, clinical question and urgency exactly as checked by the physician in s2c, signed once and released to the lab and radiology; any change needs a new check.

tasks.previous_blocker: Tests were ordered one by one and device results retyped.
tasks.enabler_now: Order sets and device links to the record.
tasks.still_hard: Atypical presentations where standard panels mislead.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which test will change management.

reach.learn: Whether order sets change test volumes.

evidence.claim: Vitals, results, codes and medication can arrive in the record by integration.
Providers are legally responsible for careful use of AI, including testing and monitoring.

assumptions: Boundary: diagnostic procedures in the emergency department; reporting by radiology is outside.
Input contract for s2: order sets agreed by the department and kept in the record by the application team.
Input contract for s5: ECG machines and ultrasound devices linked to the record; about 80% of bedside devices are; s5 is priced at that share.

Selection, procedures, interpretation and the order check and release keep their full time. s2 keeps 60 because the order set fills the standard panel; s5 keeps 80 because only device measurements fill in and the physician writes the findings.

incremental.description: Emergency physician reviews order sets with colleagues yearly.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most patients need custom orders (s2 keeps 85) and half of the devices are not linked (s5 keeps 90) (1.9); high: order sets fit common complaints and 80% of devices are linked (4.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Look up vital signs and laboratory data, evaluate them with the patient to determine emergency intervention needs and priority of treatment, and record the priority and orders.

steps.what: Emergency physician looks up vital signs and laboratory data across screens
Emergency physician evaluates the patient's vital signs and laboratory data to determine intervention needs and priority of treatment
Emergency physician records the priority of treatment
Emergency physician enters the orders: one by one today, from order sets after the change
Emergency physician checks the final orders: patient, interventions, doses and urgency against the priority decided
Emergency physician signs the checked orders, releasing them to nurses, the lab and radiology

tasks.design: The department's overview board shows each patient's latest vital signs from the monitors and lab results with abnormal values marked, so the physician sees them on one screen. Evaluating and setting priority stay fully with the physician; no software triages patients. The physician records the priority as today; orders use the order sets, and the physician checks them and signs them once.

approvals.approved_version: The orders exactly as checked by the physician in s3c, signed once for this patient and released to nurses, the lab and radiology; any change needs a new check.

tasks.previous_blocker: Vitals and results sat on separate screens and monitors.
tasks.enabler_now: Department overview boards fed by monitors and the lab system.
tasks.still_hard: Patients whose numbers look fine but who are deteriorating.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a patient looks wrong before the numbers do.

reach.learn: Whether the shared board speeds escalation.

evidence.claim: AI for emergency triage of patients is an AI Act Annex III high-risk use; the board only shows data.
Results can arrive in the record by integration.

assumptions: Boundary: deciding interventions and priority; carrying them out is outside.
Input contract for s1: monitors in treatment bays linked to the record and lab results from the lab system; about 80% of bays have linked monitors; s1 is priced at that share.

Evaluation, recording the priority, and checking and signing orders keep their full time. s1 keeps 60 because the board shows data from about 80% of bays; s3o keeps 75 because order sets fill standard orders.
unknowns: Share of bays with linked monitors.
research_questions: Is time to treatment shorter for urgent patients?

incremental.description: Emergency physician reports wrong or missing values on the board.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few bays have linked monitors (s1 keeps 80) and few orders fit a set (s3o keeps 95) (4.3); high: 80% linked bays and order sets as designed (10.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Gather the patient's history from records and other providers, analyze records, examination information and test results to diagnose medical conditions, and record the diagnosis and reasoning.

steps.what: Emergency physician gathers the patient's history from records, letters and other hospitals
Emergency physician analyzes examination information and test results to diagnose medical conditions
Emergency physician records the diagnosis, its code and the reasoning

loop.input: The diagnosis text the physician typed.
loop.output: Suggested diagnosis codes from the hospital's thesaurus.
loop.check: Suggestions come only from the national thesaurus, matched to the typed diagnosis; the physician reads each code's description against the diagnosis and picks or rejects it; no code is saved without the physician's choice, and unclear matches are coded by hand.
loop.why_not_simpler: Physicians describe the same diagnosis in many ways.

tasks.design: One summary view in the record shows problem list, medication, recent letters and results, including data exchanged from other hospitals and the pharmacy with the patient's consent, instead of opening each document. Diagnosing stays fully with the physician. The physician writes the diagnosis and reasoning as today; when the diagnosis is typed, code suggestions from the thesaurus appear and the physician picks one.
tasks.previous_blocker: History was spread over documents, other hospitals and phone calls.
tasks.enabler_now: Record summary views, regional data exchange and code suggestions.
tasks.still_hard: Patients with no records who cannot speak.
tasks.human_edge: Putting an unusual combination of signs together.

reach.learn: Whether codes chosen at the source need less correction.

evidence.claim: A practice tool drafts referral letters and suggests ICPC, ICD-10 and SNOMED codes.
Solely automated care decisions need a legal basis; the physician decides.

assumptions: Boundary: diagnosing in the emergency department; treatment is outside.

Input contract for s1: records from other hospitals and pharmacies available through regional exchange with the patient's consent, about 60% of patients; others need calls; s1 is priced at that share.
Diagnosis keeps its full time. s3 keeps 85 because only looking up the code goes; writing the diagnosis and reasoning stays.
unknowns: Share of patients with exchangeable records.
research_questions: Are medication errors at admission fewer?

already_counted.description: Emergency physician rejects wrong code suggestions.

incremental.description: Emergency physician asks patients for consent to retrieve outside records.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few patients' outside records come through the exchange (s1 keeps 85) and suggestions rarely fit (s3 keeps 95) (4.7); high: 60% of patients covered and suggestions fit (10.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Prepare the handover summary, consult with hospitalists and other professionals such as social workers regarding admission, continued observation, transition of care or discharge, agree the disposition and record it.

steps.what: Emergency physician prepares the handover summary of the emergency course
Emergency physician consults with hospitalists and social workers regarding admission, observation or discharge
Emergency physician agrees the disposition: admission, observation, transition of care or discharge
Emergency physician records the consultation and disposition
Emergency physician checks the bed request filled from the disposition: patient, ward, level of care and urgency
Emergency physician releases the bed request to bed management: by phone and a separate form today, by one release from the disposition fields after the change

tasks.design: A handover template in the record fills vital signs, results, treatments given and times from the emergency course, and the physician adds the assessment and question. Consulting and agreeing the disposition stay human. The physician records the disposition as today; its fields fill the bed request, which the physician checks and releases once to bed management.

approvals.approved_version: The bed request with patient, ward, level of care and urgency exactly as checked by the physician in s4c, released once to bed management; any change needs a new check.

tasks.previous_blocker: Handover summaries were written from scratch while the consultant waited.
tasks.enabler_now: Handover templates filled from the record.
tasks.human_edge: Arguing for a bed for a patient who needs one.

evidence.claim: A scribe study across 1,295 clinicians reported self-estimated note time falling from 6.69 to 4.72 minutes.
The dossier is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: consulting on disposition; the admitting team's work is outside.
Input contract for s1: vitals, results and treatments recorded in the record by nurses and physicians during the emergency course.

Consulting, agreeing, recording the disposition and checking the bed request keep their full time. s1 keeps 70 because the template fills facts and the physician writes the assessment and question; s4s keeps 25 for releasing the request and calls about urgent beds.
unknowns: Share of patients needing a consultation.
research_questions: Does time from decision to bed fall?

incremental.description: Emergency physician corrects missing items in the handover template.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the template misses many items (s1 keeps 85) and bed requests are still phoned (s4s keeps 70) (3.3); high: the template and request fill as designed (7.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
